body: DATE OF HEARING 05-11-2026 Appellant by:
 Mr. Shehzada Mazhar, Advocate  Kh. Haseeb Ahmad, Advocate Respondents by:
 Mr. Ali Farooq, Advocate.

 Malik Shahnawaz Noon, Advocate  Mr. Atif Amin, Advocate Ch. Sultan Mahmood,J:- The brief facts of the case are that the appellant, through its authorized representative, approached respondent No.3 for the purchase of 25,000 kilograms of Lead Ingots against a consideration of USD 35,000, which was paid through SAMBA Bank Limited. Respondent No.1 issued an Open Marine Insurance Policy bearing No.2017/03/LAFMPDO00444 dated 07.03.2017, covering the transportation of the consignment from China to Karachi. Respondent No.3 issued Performa Invoice No.ZXY-1730313 dated 13.05.2017, while the consignment was shipped under Bill of Lading No.959987119 dated 28.03.2017, with an original seal bearing No.ML-CN5093942. Upon arrival at Port Qasim, the container was delivered with a different seal bearing No. CHINA SHIPPING H-98653 and was found to weigh only 11,140 kilograms against the declared weight of 25,000 kilograms. A joint survey was subsequently conducted, which revealed that the container was empty. The appellant approached respondent No.1 Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. through telephone calls and emails dated 30.04.2017 and submitted the available documents, while also seeking settlement of its insurance claim. However, the matter remained unresolved. The appellant thereafter filed a complaint before the Federal Insurance Ombudsman on 17.09.2017, which was dismissed vide order dated 12.04.2019 on the ground of alleged pursuit of double benefits. Subsequently, the appellant instituted a suit for recovery of Rs.6,284,213/- along with liquidated damages under Section 118 of the Insurance Ordinance, 2000, bearing Insurance Application No.273/2022. The learned Insurance Tribunal, vide judgment and decree dated 22.03.2024, dismissed the suit as not maintainable, hence the instant appeal.

2. It is pertinent to mention that respondent No.1, on the basis of the available record, established that the shipping company had paid USD 35,000 to the appellant against the loss in question. The learned Insurance Tribunal dismissed the claim of the appellant on two grounds: firstly, that the claim was barred by limitation, as the loss occurred on 30.04.2017, whereas the insurance petition was instituted beyond the prescribed period of three years; and secondly, that the appellant had already received compensation from the shipping company for the same loss and, therefore, was not entitled to claim further indemnity under the principle of indemnity and subrogation.

3. Learned counsel for the appellant contends that the learned Tribunal incorrectly computed the period of limitation, as the relevant provision, namely Article 86(b) of the Limitation Act, 1908, provides two distinct points of commencement of limitation, including the date of loss and the date when the claim is rejected by the insurance company. He further contends that the matter relates to the principle of subrogation and that the appellant's claim against the insurance company is independent of the compensation received from the shipping company. According to him, the receipt Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. of compensation from a third party does not, by itself, extinguish the appellant's contractual right to claim under the insurance policy.

4. Learned counsel for the respondents vehemently opposed the appeal and supported the impugned judgment passed by the learned Insurance Tribunal. He contended that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation, as the period of limitation commenced from the date of occurrence of the loss, which admittedly took place in May 2017. He further submitted that the appellant, instead of approaching the competent forum within the prescribed period, elected to pursue a remedy before a forum lacking jurisdiction, which could not extend or revive the period of limitation.
5. Arguments heard. Record perused.

6. It is trite law that, while interpreting Article 86(b) of the Limitation Act, 1908, this Court in State Life Insurance Corporation of Pakistan through Chairman and 3 others v. Mst. Safia Begum (2001 CLC 408) and Messrs. State Life Insurance Corporation v. Mst. Kausar Jehan Begum (1982 CLC 1658) has consistently held that the period of limitation commences from the date when the insurer communicates its refusal to honour the insurance claim. Learned counsel for the appellant contends that the cause of action did not arise merely upon the occurrence of the loss on 30.04.2017; rather, it arose when respondent No.1 refused to settle the insurance claim, which refusal was reflected in the proceedings before the Federal Insurance Ombudsman, culminating in the order dated 12.04.2019. He submits that, as the insurance petition was instituted on 19.12.2020, it was well within the prescribed period of three years.

7. The above contention finds favour with this Court. In view of the principles laid down in the judgments referred to above, the period of limitation is to be reckoned from the date on which the insurer communicates its refusal to honour the claim, rather than merely from the date of occurrence of the loss. In the present case, the record reflects that the appellant pursued its insurance claim Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. before the Federal Insurance Ombudsman, and the proceedings culminated in the order dated 12.04.2019. The insurance petition was thereafter instituted on 19.12.2020, which is within three years of the said date. Thus, the petition was within the prescribed period of limitation. The learned Insurance Tribunal, therefore, erred in dismissing the claim as time-barred, and its finding on this issue is set aside.

8. The next ground urged by learned counsel for the appellant is that the principle of subrogation is applicable to the case in hand, in support whereof he has placed reliance upon Danish Elahi and 2 others v. Mariam Kamran and 3 others (PLD 2022 Sindh 362). He contends that the principle of subrogation is well recognized under the law of Pakistan, particularly in the context of insurance contracts.

9. In this case the assured person/appellant after his indemnification from the shipping company is seeking indemnification from the insurance company and while relying on the judgment of Danish Elahi’ s case and putting forth an argument that the indemnification from the shipping company is a stand alone arrangement under a different contract. We have considered the argument but we are not inclined to agree with the contention raised for reasons: firstly Danish Elahi’s case arises out of Section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act, in the case of East and West Steamship Company , distinction Section 92, provides for assignment of right to sue, and Section 135-A, provides for automatic transfer of right to recover from tort-feasor as both are distinct and separate so the principles stemming out of one are not applicable on the other per se; secondly the Lord Napier and Ettrick and another v. Hunter and others [1993] 2 WLR 42, laid down the following ingredients of the subrogation in marine insurance: (i) the right of subrogation arises automatically in favour of the insurer upon payment of the insurance claim; (ii) the assured must not 1 EAST AND WEST STEAMSHIP Co. v. QUEENSLAND INSURANCE Co. (PLD 1963 SC 663) Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. prejudice the insurer's rights of subrogation; (iii) after receiving indemnity, the assured cannot compromise or settle the claim against the wrongdoer to the prejudice of the insurer without the insurer's consent; and (iv) any recovery from the wrongdoer is, in the first instance, to be applied towards the insurer's entitlement. In plain terms, upon payment of the insurance claim, the insurer becomes entitled to pursue recovery against the carrier, notwithstanding that the insurer was not a party to the contract of carriage but this doctrine does not provide any basis to an indemnified assured person to seek indemnification from the insurer. Rather recognizes a right of the insurer in marine insurance to be indemnified by the tort-feasor.

10. There is another concept which is principle of double recovery, which states that the insured may not recover more than a full indemnity . The principle was first enunciated in Castellain v. Preston [(1883) 11 Q.B.D. 380 (Court of Appeal)]. The facts of the case were that, in July 1878, Preston and others, being owners of certain land and buildings in Liverpool, entered into an agreement to sell the property to their tenants, the Rayners. Approximately two weeks later, a portion of the buildings was damaged by fire. The owners lodged an insurance claim and, after negotiations, received £330 from their insurers. Subsequently, they completed the sale of the property and received the full purchase price from the purchasers. The Court held that, as the owners had ultimately sustained no loss, they were liable to repay the amount of £330 received from the insurers. It further observed that where, at the time of the loss, a contract exists between the insured and a third party, and such contract is duly fulfilled by the third party, no right of action arises to which the insurer could become subrogated.

11. The aforesaid principle was further explained by the Supreme Court of United Kingdom in Gatwick v. Liberty Mutual [2026] 3 AII ER 803 at 830 , wherein it was observed as follows: 2 Lord Napier and Ettrick v. Hunter [1993] AC 713 Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. “Three distinct situations may arise in this context. However, for the purposes of the present case, only the first two are relevant. In the first situation, where the insured receives compensation from a third party before being indemnified by the insurer, the insurer's liability is reduced to the extent of the amount already received. In the second situation, where the insured receives compensation from a third party after having been indemnified by the insurer, the insured is liable to account to the insurer for the amount so received, which remains subject to an equitable lien in favour of the insurer. The distinction between these two situations is merely one of timing, which, in principle, should not affect the legal consequence.” Thus, the insurer's entitlement to the benefit of a payment received from a third party does not depend upon whether such payment is received before or after indemnification by the insurer. The very foundation, in our opinion, of every rule which has been applied to insurance law is this, namely, that the contract of insurance is a contract of indemnity, and of indemnity only .

12. Moreover, Equitable subrogation was a remedy available to give effect to a proprietary right or in some cases to a cause of action. Subject to special defences, equitable subrogation served to prevent or reverse the unjust enrichment , although in this case the subrogation is not equitable but legal but infact coded version of the equity and after codification situation remains the same because no further caveats have been added to the equitable mortgage while enacting legal mortgage under Section 135-A of the ibid Act.

13. However, having already received USD 35,000 from the shipping company against the very loss forming the subject matter of the insurance claim, the appellant stand compensated and the principle of double recovery is attracted in this case, as undisputedly the Marsek, shipping company has indemnified the appellant equivalent to the sum of assured amount.

14. It is further evident from the record that the payment of USD 35,000 by Maersk Line to the appellant on 24.11.2017 is not disputed. The learned Insurance Tribunal also took into consideration the order dated 12.04.2019 passed by the Federal 3 Castellain v. Preston (1883) 11 QBD 380 4 Lowick Rose LLP Vs. Swnson Limited 2017 SCMR 907 5 East and West Steamship Co. Vs. Queensland Insurance Co. PLD 1963 SC 663 Wire Manufacturing Industry Ltd. v. Habib Insurance Company Ltd. etc. Insurance Ombudsman, wherein the factum of receipt of compensation from the shipping company against the loss in question was duly noticed. Thus, the appellant had already received the value of the consignment from the shipping company, which was the very subject matter of the insurance claim. In these circumstances, the appellant cannot be permitted to recover the same loss once again from the insurer.

15. In the circumstances, the appellant has failed to establish that the impugned judgment suffers from any illegality, misreading or non-reading of the record warranting interference by this Court. The learned Insurance Tribunal has rightly considered the admitted payment of USD 35,000 by the shipping company towards the loss in question and the legal consequences flowing therefrom under the settled principles of indemnity and subrogation. The appellant, having already received full compensation for the loss, cannot claim a second indemnity under the insurance policy. The findings recorded by the learned Tribunal, therefore, call for no interference. Consequently, the instant appeal, being devoid of merit, is dismissed.
(Malik Waqar Haider Awan) (Ch. Sultan Mahmood)
